_note: Human air traffic control timings used in docs/26 and scripts/task_latency_report.py. kind SOURCED = a published figure about air traffic control whose full text was read; DERIVED = arithmetic from a SOURCED figure; CROSS_DOMAIN = a published figure from another field (conversation, typing, driving), used only as a rough bracket and never as the ATC figure; MODELLED = our own arithmetic with stated assumptions and no citation; NOT_MEASURED = no figure found, so no comparison is made. Nothing here is a measurement of Unstep's users.

items.task: Pilot starts the readback after the instruction ends
items.source: Lutz, M., Chatterji, G. and Idris, H. (2022), 'Characterization of Response Times based on Voice Communication and Traffic Surveillance Data', NASA Ames Research Center / Crown Consulting, AIAA Aviation 2022 (NASA NTRS 20220007116, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20220007116). Readback delay = end of the controller's transmission to the start of the pilot's readback; average 0.639 s over clearances on KLAX approach, center and tower frequencies
items.note: One day of recordings (2022-03-01) in the Los Angeles area, a few hundred clearances; the pilot's side, not the controller's

items.task: Notice that a call was stepped on
items.source: Prinzo, O. V. and McClellan, M. (2005), 'Terminal Radar Approach Control: Measures of Voice Communications System Performance', FAA Civil Aerospace Medical Institute, DOT/FAA/AM-05/19 (https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/58248): blocked, stepped-on or clipped transmissions in 1.16% of sampled transmissions at five of the busiest TRACONs; 'No alerting system was detected for stepped-on or clipped transmissions through waveform analysis'. For completely blocked transmissions an audible alarm (the spoken word 'blocked' or heterodyning) typically alerted the controller, and in 94.74% of those instances the controller repeated the transmission or asked for a repeat. Separately, AIN (2025-08-04, https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2025-08-04/ntsb-dc-midair-hearing-panel-3-covers-frequency-issues): at the NTSB hearing on the 2025 DCA midair, Clark Allen, then operations manager at the KDCA tower, answered 'There's nothing' when asked to confirm that a controller has no way to know a transmission was stepped on
items.note: So a fully blocked call usually raises an alarm and gets repeated; a stepped-on call has no alert. Time to notice: not measured by either source
items.verified: full text of the CAMI report and the AIN article read 2026-10-25

items.task: Recover a lost instruction by saying again
items.source: Derived: 1.5 s for the pilot to notice and key up (CROSS_DOMAIN, Green 2000, driver response to a surprise, see below) + the request 'Tower, Cessna one two three, say again' (10 syllables, 1.6 s at 6.1 syllables per second) + the controller's repeat (13 syllables, 2.1 s) + two 0.3 s gaps (our assumption). The 1.5 s is not an aviation figure
items.note: Only if someone noticed the garble
items.verified: components cited as noted; the total is our arithmetic

items.task: Speak a clearance on the radio
items.source: Derived from the 6.1 syllables per second above: 'Cessna one two three, cleared for takeoff runway three three' is 13 syllables, so about 2.1 s. The earlier 250 ms per word was our assumption and is dropped. Cited context: Prinzo and McClellan (2005) found an average transmission at the five busiest TRACONs lasted 2568 ms of voice, over all messages
items.note: Parity expected: speaking takes as long as the words take to say
items.verified: derived from a source whose abstract was read; the 2568 ms figure read in the full CAMI text

items.task: Find the FAA paragraph that governs an instruction
items.note: Controllers work from memory and training; there is nothing to compare against

items.source: none verified. Only search snippets mentioned EUROCONTROL and FAA material on readback and hearback errors; nothing was read in full, so no claim is made
items.note: A rate problem, not a speed problem

items.source: Nitta, H., Okazaki, H. and Klinger, W. (2011), 'An Analysis of U.S. Air Traffic Controllers' Speech Speed Rates', University of Shiga Prefecture (https://www.usp.ac.jp/user/usp/english/kenkyusha/ronbun/2011/2011-I-Klinger.pdf): median 6.1 syllables per second for controllers talking to pilots at three American international airports; the same paper cites 5.1 in movies and 4.7 in news, and that non-native listeners missed 21.2% of words at 6 syllables per second and 32.7% at 7
items.verified: full text of the abstract read 2026-10-25; the body was not read
items.note: Controllers only; one study, three airports

items.task: A person's response time to an unexpected event
items.source: Green, M. (2000), 'How Long Does It Take to Stop? Methodological Analysis of Driver Perception-Brake Times', Transportation Human Factors 2(3), 195-216 (https://doi.org/10.1207/STHF0203_1): about 0.7 s when the signal is expected, about 1.25 s for an unexpected but common signal, about 1.5 s for a surprise. Driving, not aviation
items.verified: abstract only, seen through search results of the publisher page; full text not read (the publisher page returned 403)
items.note: Used only as a bracket for the pilot's reaction in the say-again cycle

items.source: Yuan, J., Liberman, M. and Cieri, C. (2006), 'Towards an Integrated Understanding of Speaking Rate in Conversation', Interspeech 2006 (https://www.ldc.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/interspeech2006-towards-integrated-understanding.pdf): overall average 196 words per minute in English conversational telephone speech (individual conversations 111 to 291)

Dhakal, V., Feit, A. M., Kristensson, P. O. and Oulasvirta, A. (2018), 'Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes', CHI 2018 (https://doi.org/10.1145/3173574.3174220): average 51.56 words per minute (SD 20.2) across 168,000 volunteers
items.note: General typists; says nothing about controllers

items.task: Write or say a short explanation
items.source: no ATC figure. A bracket from other fields only: a 60-word note takes about 70 s to type at 51.56 words per minute and about 18 s to say at 196 words per minute (both CROSS_DOMAIN, above)
items.note: Not a measurement of how long a controller takes
